title: Maximum Number of Upgradable Servers
statement:
There are `n` data centers. Data center `i` owns `count[i]` servers, upgrading one of its servers costs `upgrade[i]`, selling one of its servers earns `sell[i]`, and it starts with `money[i]` to spend.

Inside a data center you may sell any number of its servers and put the proceeds, together with its starting money, toward upgrades of the servers you keep. A sold server can no longer be upgraded, and money never moves from one data center to another.

Return an array `answer` of length `n` in which `answer[i]` is the greatest number of servers data center `i` can upgrade.
signature: int[] maxUpgrades(int[] count, int[] upgrade, int[] sell, int[] money)
notes:
## Intuition

Data centers are independent, so solve one at a time. If we upgrade `x` servers, keeping more than `x` is pointless: every server we do not upgrade should be sold for cash. The plan is affordable exactly when

`x · upgrade ≤ money + (count − x) · sell`, which rearranges to `x · (upgrade + sell) ≤ money + count · sell`.

So each upgrade effectively costs `upgrade + sell` out of a budget of `money + count · sell` (the money we would have after selling everything). The largest `x` is a floor division, capped at `count`. A brute force would try every `x` from `count` down; binary search on `x` also works, but the closed form is O(1).

## Approach

1. For each data center `i`, compute `budget = money[i] + count[i] · sell[i]`.
2. Compute `pricePerUpgrade = upgrade[i] + sell[i]`: the upgrade cost plus the sale we give up.
3. `affordable = floor(budget / pricePerUpgrade)`.
4. Push `min(count[i], affordable)`, since we cannot upgrade more servers than exist.

## Example 1, step by step

- Center 0: `budget = 8 + 4 · 4 = 24`, `pricePerUpgrade = 3 + 4 = 7`, `affordable = 3`, `min(4, 3) = 3`. Check: sell 1 server for 4, have 12, upgrade 3 for 9.
- Center 1: `budget = 9 + 3 · 2 = 15`, `pricePerUpgrade = 5 + 2 = 7`, `affordable = 2`, `min(3, 2) = 2`.

The answer is `[3, 2]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): constant work per data center.
- Space: O(1) beyond the output array.

## Pitfalls

- `count[i] · sell[i]` can reach 10^10, which overflows a 32-bit `int`; use `long` in Java or `long long` in C before dividing.
- Cap the result at `count[i]`: with lots of starting money the formula can exceed the number of servers.
- Do not divide only by `upgrade[i]`: each upgraded server is also a server you did not sell, so it costs `upgrade + sell`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `answer` | the result, one entry per data center |
| `i` | index of the current data center |
| `budget` | money available if every server were sold |
| `pricePerUpgrade` | real cost of one upgrade: its price plus the lost sale |
| `affordable` | how many upgrades the budget covers |

narration.2: Collect one result per data center.
narration.4: Handle each data center on its own, since money cannot move between them.
narration.5: Pretend every server is sold: this is the most money the center could ever have.
narration.6: Upgrading a server costs its price and also the sale we give up by keeping it.
narration.7: The budget covers this many upgrades at that effective price.
narration.8: We cannot upgrade more servers than exist, so cap the count and record it.
narration.10: Return the maximum upgrades for every data center.
